Where it began

Wasim Akram was born in Lahore on 3 June 1966 and went to Islamia College in the city. He learned the game with a taped tennis ball, and a friend, Khalid Mahmood, helped him into the Ludhiana Gymkhana club. Only weeks before he played for Pakistan he was an unknown club bowler who had not even made his college side.

Then came the national trials at the Gaddafi Stadium. For two days he waited without a bowl. On the third he got his chance, and Javed Miandad saw enough to insist that he be picked.

The player

His Test debut came against New Zealand in 1985, and in only his second Test he took ten wickets. He went on to play 104 Tests and take 414 wickets at 23.62, a Pakistan record, with 25 five-wicket innings and five ten-wicket matches. He captained Pakistan in 25 Tests and won 12 of them.

The 1992 World Cup final against England was perhaps his finest hour. He hit 33 from 19 balls, removed Ian Botham early, and later, with the ball reversing, bowled Allan Lamb and Chris Lewis with successive deliveries. He was named man of the match.

What made him special

He bowled with real pace and a very quick arm, swung the ball both ways, and could bowl round or over the wicket equally well. He was a master of reverse swing, so he was often at his most dangerous when the ball was old and the batsmen thought the worst was over. With Waqar Younis he formed the two Ws, one of the great fast-bowling pairs. Of his four international hat-tricks, two came in Tests, in back-to-back matches of the same series. Viv Richards rated him the best fast bowler he faced after Dennis Lillee.

As a batsman he loved to swing the bat, and his critics wished he had valued his wicket a little more. He answered them in 1996 at Sheikhupura with 257 not out against Zimbabwe, a record for a Test number eight, with 12 sixes in the innings.

Away from the middle

He played county cricket for Lancashire from 1988 to 1998, where the crowds sang Wasim for England, and he captained them to two one-day trophies in 1998. Wisden named him a Cricketer of the Year in 1993 and, in 2013, picked him in its all-time Test World XI. He joined the ICC Hall of Fame in 2009 and received the Hilal-e-Imtiaz in 2019. After playing he became a television commentator and a coach, helping young fast bowlers in India and Pakistan, and in 2022 he published a memoir, Sultan, written with Gideon Haigh.

And finally

In 2003 he won a Lux Style Award as the most stylish sports person, which suggests he could make even a long spell in the heat look elegant.
